data.summary: Observed 2026-10-16 in worktree fix-decision-extends-drops-globs while load average was ~550: 'git merge main' took 22m because the post-merge hook ran 'ddflow pins regenerate --after-merge' (which ran pytest tests/golden --snapshot-update serially), and after it finished 'git status' showed 'MM README.md' (git diff --stat: README.md 6473 lines changed, +6472) and ' D' for tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_mcp_tools.ambr, test_golden_outputs.ambr, test_uc_surf_reporting_pin.ambr (and test_golden_search.ambr emptied by 355 lines), plus tests/test_uc_surf_setup_ops_transcript.py failing. A second manual 'ddflow pins regenerate' printed 'golden-snapshots: re-recorded' and left the tree with README alone damaged; after 'git checkout HEAD -- README.md' a third 'ddflow pins regenerate' reported all pins current and the tree was clean. So a regeneration that overlaps with other work (or is interrupted by load/timeouts) is not atomic: it must write each pin to a temp file and rename, and refuse to leave a tree where README grows past its generator's output. Expected: the after-merge hook is idempotent and never leaves a damaged working tree.

chunk_findings.detail:
The hint is attributed to the first glob flag that merely *appears* in `argv`, not to the flag whose value is actually being followed by the stray word. The guard

    if flag in argv and argv[argv.index(flag) + 2 : argv.index(flag) + 3] and stray:

only checks that *some* token exists two slots after `--globs`; it never checks that the unrecognized words belong to that flag. Concretely, with `ddflow update --globs 'src/**' --tags a b`, argparse raises `unrecognized arguments: b` (since `--tags` takes one value), but `--globs` is in `argv`, `argv[index("--globs")+2]` is `--tags` (truthy) and `stray == ['b']`, so the function rewrites the error to

    --globs takes ONE value, a comma-separated list (--globs src/**,--tags), or the flag repeated; not space-separated words

which is both misattributed (the offending flag is `--tags`) and actively suggests a bogus usage: `--globs src/**,--tags` would install a literal `--tags` glob. A user following the printed suggestion on a perfectly valid `--tags` problem gets a silently wrong glob set. The same happens for any input where a stray token follows some other flag while `--globs` earlier in `argv` happens to be followed by two more tokens (e.g. `--globs a --needs x y`, `--globs a --priority 1 2`). The adjacency of the stray words to the flag's value needs to be verified (or the flag identified from the position of the unrecognized words) before emitting the hint.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/argtypes.py:glob_list_hint

chunk_findings.detail: The glob hint is computed from the *process's* command line (`sys.argv`) rather than from the argument vector the parser is actually parsing. `ArgumentParser.error` runs whenever `parse_args` / `parse_known_args` is called with an explicit list — which is what tests and any in‑process/embedded caller do (this module's own header notes the registry feeds the agent/MCP surface too: `AS_AGENT ... (see mcp.py)`). Concretely, a programmatic call such as `parser.parse_args(["update", "--globs", "x", "--bogus"])` executed inside a process whose `sys.argv` is `["ddflow-serve", "--transport", "stdio"]` (or pytest's argv) will feed `["--transport", "stdio"]` to `glob_list_hint`; it then finds no `--globs`/`--add-globs`/`--remove-globs` token and silently drops the hint the change was added to produce. Conversely, if the host argv happens to contain such a token, the hint is appended to an unrelated error. The parser already knows, or should be given, the argv it is parsing (e.g. store it when `parse_args` is entered); reading `sys.argv` makes the new hint unreliable in every non‑top‑level‑CLI invocation.

titles: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `super().error(glob_list_hint(message, sys.argv[1:]))` in the parser's `error` override

chunk_findings.detail:
The override materializes the caller's argument iterable into `self._argv` and then delegates the *original* `args` object to `argparse.ArgumentParser.parse_known_args`:

```python
def parse_known_args(self, args=None, namespace=None):
    self._argv = list(sys.argv[1:] if args is None else args)
    return super().parse_known_args(args, namespace)
```

Base argparse accepts any iterable here — its first statement is `args = list(args)` (CPython `argparse.py`, present in 3.9–3.13) — but it must be allowed to consume the iterable itself. `list(...)` on a one-shot iterator (generator, `map`, `filter`, `dict_keys`-style view over a stream) drains it, so the iterator handed to `super()` is already empty and the base implementation converts it to `[]`. Concrete failure: `parser.parse_known_args(iter(["--globs", "src/**"]))` previously parsed the flag and value; with this change the parser sees no arguments and instead fails with the "required arguments are missing" error path, while `self._argv` (used by the new `glob_list_hint`) still holds the words that were never parsed. Before this diff the call worked; the fix is to delegate the materialized list (`super().parse_known_args(self._argv if args is not None else None, namespace)`) rather than re-passing `args`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py — `_Parser.parse_known_args` override

The commit hook refusal ('staged paths are not covered by a lease you hold') and the claim output print 'ddflow update <ID> --globs ...' / 'ddflow claim <ID> --globs ...'; --globs REPLACES the list, so an agent following it drops every glob it holds (it hit exactly this widening a lease three times). data.body: Found by fleet-smallcli adding --add-globs/--remove-globs: ddflow update is built in TWO places, surfaces/cli.py:cmd_item_update (what the CLI runs) and the Command.call lambda in surfaces/declared/queue.py (what MCP runs). A new field had to be threaded through both; the CLI one first silently ignored it ('nothing to change: every field was left unset'). Make the CLI path use the declared call (or share one ItemEdit builder) so a field cannot be added to one and forgotten in the other. A parity test that builds ItemEdit through both paths from the same args would catch drift.
